in the first letter of John: "This is the victory that overcomes
the world, our faith" (5: 4).
Perhaps in these days we understand better than formerly
the longing which the early Christians felt for "that day"
the day spelling the end of time, the "dear last day" as
Luther used to call it. Of this day Jesus says: "In that day
you will ask me no questions", by which He means that then
all tormenting questions will be silenced, all oppressive
problems solved. In fact it is the very essence of joy that, when
it envelops our being, questioning ceases; all becomes clear
for us, self-explanatory. In an exposition of the words of
Jesus about the lilies of the field and the birds of the air,
Kierkegaard describes the latter as the great "teachers of
joy" for the simple reason that they ask no questions and
know no cares.
And is it suggested that this day, the "day" on which we
shall no more ask questions, is to become for us a present
reality? Is that joy which no one can take from us destined
to be ours, we people who—especially just now—are filled
with questioning and anxious care and every sort of distress?
To be sure, gleams of joy and sunshine are granted us now
and then. But we know too, as Hölderlin says: "Joy flashes
across our path from time to time, but it does not properly
belong to mortal beings." And we also understand the cry
of the poet who in the moment of fulfilled joy implores death
quickly to snatch him away: "Now am I blessed! pierce my
heart now!" (C. F. Meyer); for the poet knows that the
moment of joy will vanish, it will fade into the grey light of
common day, life will once more be filled with questioning
and anxious care.
II
What then is the joy which no man can take from us? It is
no joy connected with anything which this world and life
within it can bestow, even the most precious and highest
things of this world. It is a joy imparted by what lies beyond
